{
  "needed": true,
  "prompt": "Scope (frontend-only): implement UI and client-side data-handling so that ordinary (non-owner, non-superuser) users never see other users' resources when the backend enforces the described behavior. Do not change backend; rely only on the explicit API facts below.

Preserved API facts (explicit — must be assumed exactly as stated):
- For ordinary users, when they attempt GET, PUT or DELETE on another user's existing item, the backend will return HTTP 404 with response body detail="Item not found". 
- When the item truly does not exist, the backend will return the same HTTP 404 and same detail="Item not found" response. 
- Owner and superuser permissions are unchanged by this behavior (they retain their previous access). 
- The list endpoint continues to return only items visible to the current user (server-side filtering remains in place).

Frontend implementation requirements and concrete instructions (covering every applicable requirement and preserved constraint):
1) Global handling rule
- Treat any HTTP 404 response on item-level GET, PUT or DELETE as a canonical Not Found for the current user. The UI must not differentiate whether the 404 came from "item does not exist" or "item exists but belongs to another user". Both must produce identical visible behavior and messaging.
- Do not display or reveal any data that would indicate the resource exists for another user (no leaked details from error messages, response bodies, or caches).

2) Unified UX messaging
- For 404 responses on item-level GET/PUT/DELETE, display a neutral "Item not found" message (use the backend text exactly or your localized equivalent), and offer navigation back to the item list. Do not show "Permission denied", "Forbidden", or any owner/ownership clues.
- Implement a single NotFound UI (component/page/modal) used for these cases so the experience is consistent.

3) Detail (GET) requests
- Always perform a network GET to the item detail endpoint when navigating to a detail or edit page. Do not show cached detail data without a successful network verify first.
- If GET returns 200: render the returned item normally (owners and superusers will still see their data). If GET returns 404: discard any cached item detail, show the NotFound UI, and remove the item from local caches/stores if present.
- If GET returns other errors (500/timeout): show a neutral error message for server errors; do not conflate these with 404 handling.

4) Update (PUT/PATCH) requests
- For update flows that use optimistic UI, disable or guard optimistic commits when the update target is user-owned critical info; otherwise ensure immediate revert logic is in place if the request returns 404.
- When a PUT/PATCH returns 200/204: accept the response per normal.
- When a PUT/PATCH returns 404: treat as Not Found — revert any optimistic changes, remove the item from local store, display the NotFound UI or notification "Item not found", and redirect user to their item list if they are on an edit page.
- Do not display permission hints or details about the owning user.

5) Delete (DELETE) requests
- When DELETE returns 200/204: remove item from UI/store and show success per normal.
- When DELETE returns 404: treat as Not Found — remove the item from UI/store if still present (it is not visible to the current user), show the NotFound UI or a neutral notification "Item not found", and do not surface authorization details. Do not show an error that indicates the server is hiding existence for ownership reasons.

6) Lists and client-side caching
- Always source the master list from the server list endpoint (the backend guarantees it includes only the current user's visible items). Do not reconstitute or display items that are not returned by that list endpoint.
- If you persist an item list in local cache (store, localStorage, IndexedDB), reconcile with the server list on navigation or periodic sync: any cached item not present in the server-provided list should be removed from displayed lists and caches (do not present it to the user).
- If a cached list contains an item and a subsequent detail GET returns 404 for that item, remove it from the cache and UI immediately and show NotFound behavior if user was viewing it.

7) Authorization & UI affordances
- Continue to show edit/delete UI controls to users only according to the existing client-side authorization rules you already use for owners/superusers. Do not change those controls because of the new 404 behavior; however, be prepared to handle 404 responses when a non-owner attempts an action (the server will return 404).
- If the client uses any pre-checks (role checks, ownership flags), keep them; but always gracefully handle server-side 404s for the three operations.

8) Error handling and logging
- Log 404 occurrences in client-side diagnostics (for developers) with full request context, but never surface logs to users that could indicate another user's existence.
- For user-facing messages, always use the neutral NotFound UI/message described above for 404s; for other status codes use their appropriate messages.

9) Navigation behavior
- If a user is viewing an item detail or edit page and receives a 404 from GET/PUT/DELETE, immediately redirect them to the item list (or display the NotFound UI with a clear button to return to the list). Do not remain on the detail/edit screen displaying stale data.

10) Tests to add (frontend):
- Unit/integration tests that assert: GET detail 404 triggers NotFound UI and clears cache; PUT 404 reverts optimistic update (or cancels update) and clears cache; DELETE 404 removes item from list and shows NotFound message.
- E2E tests that simulate: list contains only user's items; navigating to an item for which GET returns 404 shows NotFound and does not leak data.

11) Implementation checklist (developer tasks)
- Implement a central HTTP response handler that interprets 404 for item-level endpoints as NotFound (apply to GET/PUT/DELETE). Keep other handlers unchanged.
- Reuse single NotFound UI component for all these 404 cases.
- Ensure client caches/stores (Redux, Vuex, MobX, localStorage) remove items when 404 received for that item.
- Ensure optimistic updates are reverted on 404 for PUT/PATCH.
- Ensure DELETE 404 causes removal from UI/store and NotFound UX.
- Add unit/integration/E2E tests for the three operations.

12) Minimal code patterns / pseudocode (translate to your stack):
- fetchDetail(id):
    response = await GET /items/{id}
    if response.status == 200: render response.body
    else if response.status == 404: clearCache(item id); showNotFound(); redirectToList();
    else: showServerError();

- updateItem(id, payload):
    // if optimistic: save previous state
    response = await PUT /items/{id} payload
    if response.status in (200,204): applyResponse();
    else if response.status == 404: revertOptimistic(); clearCache(id); showNotFound(); redirectToList();
    else: showServerError();

- deleteItem(id):
    response = await DELETE /items/{id}
    if response.status in (200,204): removeFromStore(id); showSuccess();
    else if response.status == 404: removeFromStore(id); showNotFound();
    else: showServerError();

Notes and constraints to follow strictly
- Do not attempt to interpret 404 as a permission error in the UI for these cases. The explicit requirement is that ordinary users see 404/not-found and must not be shown resource existence or ownership clues.
- Preserve owner and superuser behavior: nothing in front-end should block owners or superusers from their existing access flows; that will be enforced by the server and the above handling will still allow 200 responses for owners/superusers.
- Do not assume any other server behaviors beyond the explicit facts above.

Deliverable: implement the above changes in your frontend codebase: centralize 404 handling for item-level GET/PUT/DELETE, remove stale/cached items on 404, display a unified NotFound UI, and add tests to verify behavior. Ensure no UI flows reveal information about resources owned by other users."
}
